The passage weighs single-use bags (wasteful to make, harmful as litter) against stronger bags (need far more resources to make, but reused). The lesson is that a fair comparison must look at manufacturing, how long a product is used, and disposal — E.
A, B, C and D go well beyond what is said.
2: The argument says lone students should avoid the lake at night because the University can't control safety there. That only works if the City Council's safety measures are missing or worse than the University's — D.
3:
The writer asks 'aren't we being just the teeniest bit irrational?' and argues horse is no different from other meats. The main claim is that the British reaction is a little irrational — D.
A is the reason; B is the rival chef's view; C and E are stronger than the writer's claim.
4:
The argument assumes lower demand now means less poaching. C breaks this: poachers stockpile ivory to sell later, so falling demand need not reduce killing.
A and E would support a decline; B and D don't address it.
5: Legitimacy comes from consent, and the argument concludes more voting means more legitimacy. That assumes voting counts as consent to the system — B.
6: The argument says appointed officials are captive to the politicians who appoint them, so they should be elected. A weakens the premise: once appointed, they act against those politicians' goals, so they are not captive.
7: The argument moves from police overreach and the risk of street dealing to 'we should simply accept drugs in nightclubs'. It treats these as the only options, ignoring others (better policing without overreach, etc.) — A.
8:
The officers ended the strike to police the carnival and received a 6.5% rise. So the carnival will be policed by a full-strength force on improved pay — B.
A, C, D and E go beyond the passage (C is only the Government's claim).
9: The news stories claimed animals understand mathematics better. The writer's answer is that pigeons simply learnt from experience. That only refutes the stories if learning from experience isn't a mathematical process — E.
10:
The argument says zoos should close because they keep animals in poor conditions. E gives a strong reason to keep zoos: they save endangered species by breeding and reintroducing them.
B is weaker (education is already dismissed as misleading); A, C and D don't tackle the conclusion as directly.
11:
The milk policy is criticised (it treats all children the same and ignores benefits of full-fat milk), leading to: 'It is another example of the Government interfering unhelpfully' — C.
A and B are reasons; D and E aren't stated.
12: Happier Swiss areas have more referendums, so the argument says referendums cause happiness. It assumes referendums are the only reason those Swiss are happier — B.
13:
After explaining the harm of counterfeit medicines, the passage says efforts have neglected them and 'This should now be remedied': more effort should go into tackling them — E.
A, B, C and D are supporting points.
14: Areas with more trees have less asthma, so the argument recommends planting trees. C gives another explanation: those areas are farther from factories and traffic, which trigger asthma — so trees may not be the cause.
15:
The scheme improves homeless people's lives and saves about £1000 a month each. So individual caseworkers should be assigned — A.
B, C, D and E are not conclusions the passage supports.
16: The argument assumes eating more fruit and veg means eating less meat and dairy, which would hurt farmers. That need not follow — people could eat more fruit and veg as well — E.
17:
Besides reducing flood flow, the passage says these schemes improve water quality, prevent erosion and store carbon. So their benefits go beyond flood risk — B.
A, C, D and E are not supported.
18:
Fish farming is cleaner than cattle, but carnivorous fish like salmon deplete wild fish. So it would be better for the environment if more farmed fish were non-carnivorous — D.
A and E are recommendations that go further; B and C are not supported.
19:
Spinal manipulation helps some, but over half get side effects and hundreds have been seriously harmed. So chiropractic may do more harm than good — B.
A is too strong; C, D and E aren't supported.
20: The argument says too few women in senior posts means the most able are not always promoted. That assumes women are as able as men to fill these roles — D.
21: The argument claims prejudice against women coders, because women's acceptance rates fell when their gender was shown. E shows men's rates fell too when gender was revealed — so the drop isn't about women.
22: The spokesperson says prisons are too comfortable to deter, citing reoffending. That assumes less comfortable prisons would stop reoffending — A.
23: The argument says legal sales would increase transplants. That assumes some people in the UK would actually sell a kidney — B.
24: The argument says shooting is necessary for conservation. E weakens 'necessary': reintroducing top predators would conserve better.
25: The argument says stopping aggressive parenting would remove much violence. D gives a common cause of both — poverty — so aggressive parenting may not be the cause of later violence.
26: The argument calls the traders hypocrites for avoiding tax as they criticise Starbucks. A weakens it: their aim is protest, to push the government to act, not to profit from avoidance.
27:
Conclusion: rows should be standard because they help concentration. E adds another advantage of rows: everyone can see visual aids more easily.
C weakens; A is neutral; B and D are weak.
28: The argument says unpaid placements favour the rich because poorer people can't go without pay for long. C weakens it: many placements last only a day or two, which poorer young people can manage.
29:
Exact sciences make reliable predictions; economists failed to predict the 2008 crash and LTCM collapsed. So economics is not a science like chemistry or physics — C.
A, B, D and E go too far.
30: The argument says honest conversations could reduce turnover — people leave because of unspoken expectations they never discuss. It assumes people currently aren't honest about why they leave (they quit instead of raising the problem) — C.
